questions.question: Differentiate between autecology and synecology. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Differentiate between autecology and synecology. [U] [CO2]
  • Autecology: It is the subdivision of ecology which deals with the ecological study of one species
  • of organism throughout its life in relation to the ecological habitat factors like the life history,
  • population dynamics, behaviour, home range etc. thereby concentrating on the finer details of a
  • particular organism. It sharply focuses on a particular organism with a purpose of seeing how it
  • fits into general ecological picture.
  • For example: Relationship of an oak tree to its environment.
  • Synecology: It deals with the ecological studies of communities or entire ecosystems, describing
  • the overall energy and material flow through the system. Hence it is the study of groups of
  • organisms in relation to its environment which are associated together as a unit.
  • For example: tropical forests or deserts.
questions.source_exam: First Semester MGU-UGP/MGU-BBA/MGU-BCA Honours Examinations November 2025

questions.question: Identify the characteristics of grassland ecosystem. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Identify the characteristics of grassland ecosystem. [U] [CO3]
  • Grassland ecosystems are characterized by the dominance of grasses and herbaceous vegetation,
  • with trees being absent or sparsely distributed due to moderate and seasonal rainfall. These
  • ecosystems typically occur in regions receiving 25 –75 cm of annual precipitation, which is
  • insufficient for forest formation but adequate for sustaining extensive grass cover. Grasslands
  • support diverse faunal communities, particularly large grazing herbivores such as bison, antelope,
  • zebras, and deer, along with carnivores like lions, cheetahs, wolves, and various scavengers.
  • Burrowing animals, insects, reptiles, and ground-nesting birds are also abundant. The ecological
  • interactions within grasslands contribute to nutrient cycling, energy flow, and ecosystem stability.
questions.source_exam: First Semester MGU-UGP/MGU-BBA/MGU-BCA Honours Examinations November 2025

questions.question: Distinguish between specific and ecological mortality. / [CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• Distinguish between specific and ecological mortality. [U] [CO5]
  • Natality refers to the average number of offspring produced by a population per unit
  • time. The tendency to multiply is an in herent ability of a population. There are two
  • types of natality:
  • i) Maximum (Absolute or Potential or Physiological) natality:
  •  It is theoretical maximum production of new individuals under ideal or optimal
  • conditions. Usually it is a constant for a given population.
  •  This is never attained in nature owing to several adverse causes.
  •  For example, the maximum natality of a fish (Salmon) is 28000000 eggs in a season.
  • But all the eggs do not hatch and develop into adults because of unfavorable
  • environmental conditions.
  • ii) Ecological or realized natality : It refers to normal birth rate under actual or specific
  • environmental conditions.
  •  It is not a constant for a population but may vary with the size and fecundity of the
  • population and the physical environmental conditions.
  •  Ecological natality is always lesser than the potential natality.
questions.source_exam: First Semester MGU-UGP/MGU-BBA/MGU-BCA Honours Examinations November 2025

questions.question: Differentiate between species richness and evenness. / [CO6] [5x3 = 15]

  • region is measured on the basis of two parameters: Species richness and equitability or
  • evenness

questions.question: Describe the components of ecosystem. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe components of ecosystem. [U] [CO3]
  • An ecosystem comprises two very closely interconnected parts, called Components. These are
  • the living parts called biotic components and the non -living parts called abiotic components.
  • Biotic component is an important part of ecosystem in which energy flows in the form of food
  • from one organism to another organism within a community. Abiotic components are another
  • part of ecosystem comprising inorganic, organic, and physical or climatic components.
  • Together, these two components determine the characteristics of the ecosystem.
  • (1) Biotic Components
  • Biotic components are basically divided into following categories-
  • (i) Producers or Autotrophs
  • (ii) Consumers or Heterotrophs
  • (a) Primary consumers - herbivores
  • (b) Secondary consumers - carnivores
  • (c) Tertiary or top consumers carnivores
  • (iii) Parasites and Detrivores
  • (iv) Decomposers
  • Producers are green plants or autotrophs which synthesize their own food by the process called
  • photosynthesis.
  • Consumers are heterotrophic organisms which directly or indirectly depend on producer s for
  • energy. Energy is procured in the form of food. Consumers have been divided into three
  • categories-
  • (a) Primary consumers. These organisms are herbivores which depend upon green plants for
  • their food, e.g. cow, goat, rabbit, some insects etc.
  • (b) Secondary consumers. These are those carnivores that use herbivores as their source of
  • food, e.g. snake, frog etc.
  • (c) Tertiary consumers . These are also called top consumers and these kill and eat the
  • secondary or primary consumers. Example of top carnivores are lion, tiger, hawk etc.
  • Parasites are those organisms, which obtain their food directly from living organisms (hosts).
  • Detrivores or scavengers are small animals, which feed on dead bodies of other organisms,
  • such as termites.
  • Decomposers are generally saprophytic microbes which decompose the dead organisms, such
  • as bacteria and fungi. These decompose organic complexes into simple substances, which are
  • either mixed within the soil or evaporated to the atmosphere. These are also called micro
  • consumers.
  • Producers, consumers and decomposers remain linked together by food chain wherein each
  • category forms a trophic level.
  • ABIOTIC COMPONENTS
  • The abiotic or non -living components include the climatic and edaphic factors. The climatic
  • factors include temperature, humidity, rain and snowfall etc. The edaphic factors comprise the
  • soil and substratum. The ability of organisms to utilize, tolerate or combat the various abiotic
  • factors are different and it may limit their distribution, behavior and relationshi p with ot her

questions.question: Explain positive interspecific interactions among species. / [CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain positive interspecific interactions among species. [U] [CO5]
  • Species interactions form the basis for many ecosystem properties and processes such as
  • nutrient cycling and food webs. The interactions among the individuals of the same
  • species is known as intraspecific interaction and that among the individuals of different
  • species is called interspecific interaction. These relationships between species may be
  • beneficial to both, harmful to both or harmful to one and neutral for the other.
  • Positive Interactions:
  • Positive interactions play a critical but unde rappreciated role in ecological communities by
  • reducing physical or biotic stresses in existing habitats and by creating new habitats on which
  • many species depend.

questions.question: Identify the concept of ecotone and edge effect. / [CO6]
questions.solution_html:
• Identify the concept of ecotone and edge effect.
  • The zone where two major communities meet and blend together is known as an ecotone or a
  • tension zone. In other words, an ecotone is a transition zone between two or more communities.
  • The extent of ecotones is variable. The environmental conditions in the ecotone are
  • intermediate between the two neighboring communities. An ectone presents a situation of
  • special ecological interest. The border between forest and grassland, the transition between
  • pond and dry land, the estuarine and the bank of a stream running through a meadow are some
  • good examples of ecotone.
  • A remarkable feature of ectone is that it contains a great number of species and a higher
  • population density than either of the neighboring communities. This tendency of ectone is
  • known as edge effect or principle of edges. The species, which occur primarily or abundantly
  • in the ecotone, are often called edge species.
  • For e.g. the mangrove forests represent an ecotone between marine and terrestrial ecosystem.
  • Other examples are grassland (between forest and desert), estuary (between fresh water and
  • salt water) and riverbank or marshland (between dry and wet).
  • Features of Ecotones
  • • A sharp vegetation transition for example change in grass colours indicates an ecotone.
  • • Physiognomy: a key indicator of ecotone where the plant species differ in physical
  • appearance.
  • • Change in species is indicators of ecotone where we observe some specific organisms
  • at one side of the ecotone boundary while some other specific organism on the other
  • side.
  • • Spatial mass effect: New plant establishment or migration obscures an ecotone as they
  • cannot form self -sustaining population in different ecotone. But if survives between
  • two communities, then species richness is exhibited by the ecotone.
  • • An ecotone can reveal the space sharing efficiency of two communities and the types
  • of biomes by observing the exotic species abundance in ecotone.
  • • Best model to study diverse ecosystem.
  • • Shift in dominance represented by ecotone.
  • • Ecotone act as an ecological niche for the species colonizing at the junction called edge
  • effect.

questions.question: Explain population ecology. / [CO5] [10x2 = 20]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain population ecology. [U] [CO6]
  • Population ecology is a branch of ecology that studies the dynamics of species populations
  • and how these popul ations interact with the environment. It focuses on understanding the
  • factors that influence population size, density, distribution, growth, and structure over time. By
  • analyzing these patterns, population ecology helps explain how species survive, reproduce, and
  • respond to ecological pressures, forming the basis for wildlife management, conservation
  • biology, and environmental planning.
  • One of the fundamental concepts in population ecology is population size, which refers to the
  • total number of individuals in a given area. Population density, the number of individuals per
  • unit area or volume, provides insights into the intensity of interactions among individuals, such
  • as competition for resources or breeding opportunities. Population distribution describes how
  • individuals are spaced within their habitat —whether uniformly, randomly, or in clumps.
  • Clumped distribution is the most common, occurring when resources are unevenly distributed
  • or social behaviors promote grouping.
  • Population ecology also examines age structure, the proportion of individuals in different age
  • groups within a population. Age structure influences growth potential because younger
  • individuals contribute more to future reproduction. Closely connected to this is natality (birth
  • rate) and mortality (death rate), two demographic factors that directly determine population
  • growth. Immigration and emigration, the movement of individuals in and out of populations,
  • also play crucial roles in shaping population dynamics.
  • Population growth follows distinct patterns. Under ideal conditions—with abundant resources
  • and no limiting factors—populations grow exponentially. This is represented by the J -shaped
  • curve, indicating rapid and unchecked increase. However, such growth is rarely sustained in
  • natural environments. As resources become limited, competition intensifies, leading to logistic
  • growth, described by an S -shaped curve. The logistic model incorporates the concept of
  • carrying capacity (K), the maximum population size that the environment can support over
  • time. When population size nears the carrying capacity, growth slows and eventually stabilizes.
  • Environmental factors that regulate population size are broadly categorized into density-
  • dependent and density-independent factors. Density -dependent facto rs, such as disease,
  • predation, and competition, have stronger effects as population density increases. Density -
  • independent factors, including natural disasters and climatic conditions, affect populations
  • regardless of size. These regulatory mechanisms ens ure that populations do not grow
  • indefinitely and help maintain ecological balance.
